myths.nuance: The Falcon plate reader does not run facial recognition and Flock says none is planned. But Flock's Condor video cameras detect, follow and zoom on people, and did so to a reporter on camera in June 2026. 'No facial recognition' is true of one product, not the product line.

A Falcon takes six to twelve stills when its motion sensor fires; it does not stream or store video. Condor does stream live video, and Raven records short audio windows. Know which box is on the pole.

Flock's FAQ says the cameras have no speed-detection capability, and none is in the hardware. Speed is derivable from timestamped frames, and Flock quietly removed its 'not used to enforce traffic violations' language in December 2025.
There is no evidence a Falcon captures phone identifiers. Its Wi-Fi and Bluetooth exist for installation and battery telemetry. Phone-signal capture is a different vendor's product.

myths.claim: Only my local police can see it.
myths.nuance: Sharing is the default architecture. One Texas deputy's search in April 2025 reached 83,345 cameras in 6,809 networks. Roughly three quarters of law-enforcement customers opted into the national lookup; Flock removed federal agencies and three states from it after the reporting.

The default is now 7 days, down from 30 in August 2026, and several states cap it at 21 to 60 days. But agencies can set longer periods, and the new Evidence Mode preserves selected data with no published limit.

Flock says it has never sold customer data. On 16 February 2026 the clause 'Flock does not own and shall not sell Customer Data' was removed from its terms and a perpetual license to use customer data was added. The company describes the change as clarification.
They band onto any pole: mid-block, highway ramps, subdivision and apartment entrances, business parks, plus trailers and portable Flex units.

myths.claim: It is recording 24/7 and uploading everything.
myths.nuance: Capture is motion-triggered and uploads are bursts of crops and text, not a stream. In practice every passing vehicle trips the sensor day and night, so the distinction matters for bandwidth, not for whether your car was logged.
There is no driver-facing opt-out. An agency can add plates to its own safelist, which only affects that agency's instance; your reads remain searchable by every other network that captured them.

myths.claim: A plate cover or spray defeats it.
myths.nuance: Obscuring a plate is illegal in most states and is itself grounds for a stop. The system also describes vehicles without a readable plate, and 'covered or missing plate' is one of the attributes it indexes.

myths.claim: It cannot read temporary paper tags.
myths.nuance: Reading paper and temporary plates, and distinguishing them from permanent ones, is a marketed feature.
The on-device model also records make, body type, color, roof racks, bumper stickers, decals, damage, aftermarket wheels and hitches, and natural-language search runs over those descriptions.

Flock owns and leases the hardware at about $3,000 per camera per year and is supposed to remove it when a contract ends. Cambridge, Evanston and Verona documented cameras installed or left running after cancellation. Private HOA cameras are unaffected by a city's decision.

myths.claim: An AI decides who is a criminal.
myths.nuance: Alerts come from matching a plate against hot lists that humans maintain, and a human acts on the alert. The failure mode is worse than the myth: lists with stale or mistyped entries plus OCR error produced misread-plate rates of 71% (Roseville) and 32% (LAPD) among alerts, and wrongful stops at gunpoint.

myths.claim: The data goes to the federal government.
myths.nuance: Flock has no ICE contract. In 2025 local agencies ran thousands of searches with 'ICE' or 'immigration' as the reason, and CBP, HSI, the Secret Service and NCIS held pilot access, which Illinois found violated state law. Flock then removed federal agencies from the lookup and added a federal-sharing toggle.

myths.claim: Police need a warrant to search it.
myths.nuance: Searches run without a warrant or court order. A case number became mandatory only in August 2026 and is free text. A federal court in Norfolk held in 2026 that the network there was not yet extensive enough to be a Fourth Amendment search; the case is on appeal.

No attacker exfiltration of customer data is confirmed. In December 2025 and January 2026, more than sixty Condor cameras and several plate readers were reachable on the open internet with no authentication, exposing live feeds and archives, which Flock attributed to carrier testing.

myths.claim: It is proven to reduce crime.
myths.nuance: No large independent peer-reviewed causal study exists. Forbes found burglaries rose in a city Flock cited for an 80% drop. Agencies do document recovered vehicles and cleared cases; the question is attribution, not whether any case was ever helped.

myths.claim: It does not build a profile of anyone's movements.
myths.nuance: Flock's chief information security officer told the Oshkosh council the system creates no pattern or heat map of an individual's movement. A plate search returns every camera that saw the vehicle across the retention window, plotted on a map, which is exactly that.
More than eighty jurisdictions have left. Many immediately replaced Flock with Axon or Motorola plate readers that do the same thing, and privately owned Flock cameras keep operating.
